statement: Only people with a family history of breast cancer can develop it.
explanation_short: Family history can increase risk, but many people diagnosed have no known family history.
explanation_long: The WHO reports that about 80% of breast cancers occur in women with no specific risk factors other than sex and age.
source_name: World Health Organization — Breast cancer fact sheet

statement: Men can develop breast cancer.
explanation_short: Breast cancer is much more common in women, but men have breast tissue too and can also develop it.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — Male Breast Cancer (Patient Version)

statement: Every breast lump is cancerous.
explanation_short: Many breast lumps are benign, but a new or unusual lump should be checked by a healthcare professional.
explanation_long: The WHO notes that most breast lumps are not cancer, and that anyone with an abnormal lump should seek medical care.
source_name: World Health Organization — Breast cancer fact sheet

statement: Breast cancer always causes pain.
explanation_short: Breast cancer may not cause pain. The absence of pain does not rule it out.
explanation_long: The WHO describes a breast lump or thickening that is often without pain, and advises seeking care even if a lump does not hurt.
source_name: World Health Organization — Breast cancer fact sheet

statement: Breast cancer can occur in younger adults.
explanation_short: Risk generally increases with age, but cancer can be diagnosed at any age, including in younger adults.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — Age and Cancer Risk

statement: “I don’t have a family history, so I’m not at risk.”
explanation_short: Family history is one of many risk factors. Anyone can develop breast cancer.
explanation_long: About 80% of breast cancers occur in women with no specific risk factors other than sex and age.
source_name: World Health Organization — Breast cancer fact sheet

statement: Breast cancer only happens to women.
explanation_short: Men can develop breast cancer too, because they also have breast tissue.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — Male Breast Cancer (Patient Version)

statement: A breast lump always means cancer.
explanation_short: Many changes are not cancer, but new or persistent ones should be checked.
explanation_long: The NHS says most breast lumps are harmless, for example a fibroadenoma or a cyst, but advises always getting a lump checked by a doctor.
source_name: NHS — Breast lumps

statement: Most breast lumps turn out not to be cancer.
explanation_short: Most breast lumps are not cancer, but any new or unusual lump is still worth checking.
source_name: World Health Organization — Breast cancer fact sheet

statement: Breast cancer is contagious and can spread from person to person.
explanation_short: Cancer is not a contagious disease that spreads from person to person.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — Common Cancer Myths and Misconceptions

statement: Using antiperspirant or deodorant has been shown to cause breast cancer.
explanation_short: No scientific evidence links antiperspirants or deodorants to the development of breast cancer.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — Antiperspirants/Deodorants and Breast Cancer

statement: Knowing what is normal for your body helps you notice changes.
explanation_short: Knowing what is normal for you makes it easier to spot a change that is worth checking with a professional.
source_name: NHS — Symptoms of breast cancer in women

statement: Having a risk factor means you will definitely get breast cancer.
explanation_short: A risk factor raises the chance of disease; it does not guarantee a diagnosis.
explanation_long: Even among people who inherit a harmful BRCA1 or BRCA2 change, some never develop cancer.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — BRCA Gene Changes: Cancer Risk and Genetic Testing

statement: Breast cancer that is found and treated early is linked to fewer deaths.
explanation_short: The WHO reports that deaths are reduced when breast cancer is detected and treated early.
source_name: World Health Organization — Breast cancer fact sheet

statement: A change doesn’t always mean cancer, but a noticed change is worth checking.
explanation_short: Many breast changes have other causes, but changes that are not normal for you are worth checking with a healthcare professional.
source_name: NHS — Symptoms of breast cancer in women

statement: A new lump or swelling in the breast, chest or armpit is worth getting checked.
explanation_short: A lump or swelling in the breast, chest or armpit is one of the possible signs a healthcare professional can check.
source_name: NHS — Symptoms of breast cancer in women

statement: A change in the size or shape of a breast may need medical evaluation.
explanation_short: New or persistent breast changes should be assessed by a healthcare professional.
source_name: World Health Organization — Breast cancer fact sheet

statement: Dimpling, redness or other changes in breast skin can be a possible sign worth checking.
explanation_short: Skin changes such as dimpling, redness or pitting are listed among possible signs to get checked.
source_name: World Health Organization — Breast cancer fact sheet

statement: A nipple that turns inward or changes appearance is never worth mentioning to a doctor.
explanation_short: A change in how the nipple looks, or a nipple turning inward, is worth mentioning to a healthcare professional.
source_name: NHS — Symptoms of breast cancer in women

statement: Unexpected nipple discharge, when you’re not pregnant or breastfeeding, is worth checking.
explanation_short: Nipple discharge outside pregnancy or breastfeeding is one of the changes a healthcare professional can assess.
source_name: NHS — Symptoms of breast cancer in women

statement: If a lump doesn’t hurt, you don’t need to get it checked.
explanation_short: Breast lumps are often painless. Seek medical care for an abnormal lump even if it does not hurt.
source_name: World Health Organization — Breast cancer fact sheet

statement: Breast pain on its own is usually a sign of breast cancer.
explanation_short: Breast pain by itself is unlikely to be a symptom of cancer, though pain that doesn’t improve is still worth discussing with a doctor.
source_name: NHS — Breast pain

statement: Breast tenderness that comes and goes with periods is common.
explanation_short: Hormonal changes around periods often cause breast pain that eases when the period ends.
source_name: NHS — Breast pain

statement: Having no symptoms means breast cancer is impossible.
explanation_short: Breast cancer may be present before symptoms appear. Screening recommendations depend on age, individual risk, and local guidance.
explanation_long: Screening mammograms can find some tumours at an earlier stage, before they cause symptoms.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — Mammograms fact sheet

statement: Noticing a breast change means you definitely have cancer.
explanation_short: Many breast changes are common and have other causes. A healthcare professional can help find out what is going on.
source_name: NHS — Symptoms of breast cancer in women

statement: Men should also get a new lump near the nipple checked.
explanation_short: In men, a lump or thickening in or near the breast is the most common sign. It is worth getting checked.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — Male Breast Cancer (Patient Version)

statement: Benign conditions such as cysts can cause breast lumps.
explanation_short: Fluid-filled cysts and other benign conditions can cause lumps. A professional can tell the difference.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — Understanding Breast Changes

statement: Swelling in the armpit can be one of the possible signs of breast cancer.
explanation_short: A lump or swelling in the armpit is listed among possible signs worth checking.
source_name: NHS — Symptoms of breast cancer in women

statement: If you notice a breast change, it’s best to wait a year to see if it goes away.
explanation_short: It is important to contact a doctor if you notice any changes in your breasts.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — Understanding Breast Changes

statement: Family history is the only factor that influences breast cancer risk.
explanation_short: Age, inherited genetic variants, personal medical history, and other factors can influence risk.
explanation_long: The WHO lists increasing age, obesity, harmful use of alcohol, family history, tobacco use and postmenopausal hormone therapy among risk factors.
source_name: World Health Organization — Breast cancer fact sheet

statement: Increasing age is one of the factors linked to higher breast cancer risk.
explanation_short: Risk generally increases with age.
source_name: World Health Organization — Breast cancer fact sheet

statement: Inheriting a harmful change in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 gene can increase breast cancer risk.
explanation_short: Harmful BRCA1 and BRCA2 changes raise breast cancer risk. A healthcare provider or genetic counsellor can explain what this means.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — BRCA Gene Changes: Cancer Risk and Genetic Testing

statement: Everyone who inherits a harmful BRCA1 or BRCA2 change will develop breast cancer.
explanation_short: These changes raise risk a lot, but some people who inherit them never develop cancer.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — BRCA Gene Changes: Cancer Risk and Genetic Testing

statement: A harmful BRCA gene change can only be inherited from your mother.
explanation_short: Everyone inherits one copy of each BRCA gene from each parent, so a change can come from either parent.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — BRCA Gene Changes: Cancer Risk and Genetic Testing

statement: Drinking alcohol is linked to a higher risk of breast cancer.
explanation_short: Alcohol is linked to higher breast cancer risk, and even light drinking is associated with some increase.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — Alcohol and Cancer Risk

statement: Obesity is one of the factors associated with breast cancer risk.
explanation_short: The WHO lists obesity among factors that increase breast cancer risk.
source_name: World Health Organization — Breast cancer fact sheet

statement: Being physically active is listed as a factor that may help reduce breast cancer risk.
explanation_short: Being physically active is one of the protective factors described by the National Cancer Institute.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — Breast Cancer Prevention (Patient Version)

statement: Breastfeeding for several months is listed as a factor that can lower breast cancer risk.
explanation_short: Breastfeeding for at least several months after childbirth is listed as a protective factor.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — Breast Cancer Prevention (Patient Version)

statement: If you have no known risk factors, you cannot get breast cancer.
explanation_short: Having no known risk factors does not eliminate risk. Most cases occur in women with no specific risk factors other than sex and age.
source_name: World Health Organization — Breast cancer fact sheet

statement: Postmenopausal hormone therapy is among the factors linked to increased breast cancer risk.
explanation_short: The WHO lists postmenopausal hormone therapy among factors that increase risk. A doctor can discuss benefits and risks.
source_name: World Health Organization — Breast cancer fact sheet

statement: Tobacco use is listed among breast cancer risk factors.
explanation_short: The WHO includes tobacco use among the factors that increase breast cancer risk.
source_name: World Health Organization — Breast cancer fact sheet

statement: Nothing can guarantee you won’t get breast cancer, but some factors can reduce risk.
explanation_short: No step guarantees prevention, but protective factors such as physical activity and limiting alcohol can lower risk.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — Breast Cancer Prevention (Patient Version)

statement: This game can calculate your personal breast cancer risk.
explanation_short: This game is educational only. A healthcare provider or genetic counsellor can talk with you about your personal risk.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — BRCA Gene Changes: Cancer Risk and Genetic Testing

statement: Men who inherit a harmful BRCA2 change have a higher breast cancer risk than men in general.
explanation_short: Inherited BRCA2 changes raise breast cancer risk in men as well as women.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — BRCA Gene Changes: Cancer Risk and Genetic Testing

statement: Screening recommendations are the same for everyone.
explanation_short: Screening depends on your age, personal risk factors and medical history. A healthcare professional can advise what is right for you.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — Mammograms fact sheet

statement: Screening mammograms can find some breast cancers before they cause symptoms.
explanation_short: Mammograms can find some tumours at an earlier stage, before symptoms appear.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — Mammograms fact sheet

statement: Being called back after a mammogram means you definitely have cancer.
explanation_short: Most people who are called back for more imaging are not found to have breast cancer.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — Mammograms fact sheet

statement: A screening test can sometimes miss a cancer.
explanation_short: No screening test is perfect. False-negative results can happen, especially with dense breast tissue.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — Breast Cancer Screening (Patient Version)

statement: Dense breast tissue can make cancer harder to see on a mammogram.
explanation_short: Mammography is more likely to miss cancer in dense breasts. A doctor can explain what breast density means for you.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — Mammograms fact sheet

statement: Finding a change early doesn’t matter.
explanation_short: Noticing a change early and getting advice can lead to better outcomes. Deaths are reduced when breast cancer is found and treated early.
source_name: World Health Organization — Breast cancer fact sheet

statement: Men usually develop breast cancer at a later age than women.
explanation_short: Men of any age can get breast cancer, but it usually occurs at a later age in men than in women.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — Male Breast Cancer (Patient Version)

statement: Herbal products have been proven to cure cancer.
explanation_short: No herbal products have been shown to be effective for treating cancer. Talk to your care team before trying any supplement.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — Common Cancer Myths and Misconceptions

statement: A positive attitude alone decides whether someone gets cancer.
explanation_short: There is no convincing scientific evidence linking a person’s attitude to their risk of developing cancer.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — Common Cancer Myths and Misconceptions

statement: Having a biopsy or surgery commonly causes cancer to spread.
explanation_short: The chance that surgery causes cancer to spread is extremely low.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — Common Cancer Myths and Misconceptions

statement: If you’re worried about inherited risk, a healthcare provider or genetic counsellor can help.
explanation_short: Anyone concerned about inherited risk can discuss it with a healthcare provider or a genetic counsellor.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — BRCA Gene Changes: Cancer Risk and Genetic Testing

statement: If you feel a new lump, you should wait until your next routine screening to mention it.
explanation_short: Don’t wait: if you feel a lump in your breast, get it checked by a doctor.
source_name: NHS — Breast lumps

statement: Most cancers are caused by harmful gene changes inherited from parents.
explanation_short: Only about 5 to 10 percent of cancers are caused by harmful inherited mutations.
source_name: National Cancer Institute — Common Cancer Myths and Misconceptions

statement: A small share of breast cancers, around 0.5–1%, occur in men.
explanation_short: The WHO estimates that about 0.5–1% of breast cancers occur in men.
source_name: World Health Organization — Breast cancer fact sheet
